title: Review: Practical techniques and uncertainties; pH and Kw; Titrations and solution calculations
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AM08#t2 term and clue written for the game; PR01b#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB02#t1 term and clue written for the game; AM08#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB02#N.4, AM08#N.11, PR01a#N.12, PR01b#N.9, AB02#N.10a, AM08#N.6a, PR01a#N.13, AB02#N.6, AM08#N.13, PR01a#N.5, AB02#N.12, AM08#N.9. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Conical flask
items.clue: Vessel in which the two solutions meet, swirled over a white tile.

items.label: Hazard
items.clue: Something that could cause harm, such as a corrosive or flammable substance.

items.label: pH meter
items.clue: Gives a precise reading, usually to 0.01, after being calibrated with buffers.

items.label: Indicator
items.clue: A few drops are added so a visible change shows when the moles match the equation.

questions.stem: Hydrobromic acid, HBr, is a strong acid. What is the pH of 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ HBr(aq)?
questions.explanation: HBr ionises completely, so [H⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻³ and pH = −log₁₀(4.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.40.

questions.stem: Now the mission: vinegar. 10.0 cm³ of vinegar is titrated with 0.500 mol dm⁻³ NaOH, using phenolphthalein. The mean titre is 16.60 cm³. CH₃COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq) → CH₃COONa(aq) + H₂O(l). What is the concentration of ethanoic acid in the vinegar, in mol dm⁻³?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.500 × 0.01660 = 8.30 × 10⁻³ mol. Ratio 1 : 1, so 8.30 × 10⁻³ mol of acid. Divide by the vinegar volume, 0.0100: 0.830.

questions.stem: A student plots the volume of gas collected against time. The line of best fit is straight, but does not pass through the origin. It passes through (10 s, 14 cm³) and (50 s, 62 cm³). What is the gradient, in cm³ s⁻¹?
questions.explanation: (62 − 14) ÷ (50 − 10) = 48 ÷ 40 = 1.2. The line meets the y-axis at 2 cm³, so one point alone gives the wrong answer.

questions.stem: A student must heat a reaction mixture containing ethanol (highly flammable, boiling point 78 °C) for 30 minutes. Which plan best controls the risk?

options.text: Heat it over a Bunsen burner on a low flame, in a fume cupboard.
Heat it over a Bunsen burner, wearing gloves and eye protection.
Heat it under reflux, using a water bath or an electric heater.
Heat it in an open beaker so that the vapour can escape.

questions.explanation: No naked flame, and the condenser returns ethanol vapour to the flask, so little escapes.

questions.stem: At 298 K, solution P has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and solution Q has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. How does [OH⁻] in P compare with [OH⁻] in Q?

options.text: It is 100 times larger in P than in Q.
It is the same, as acid has no effect on [OH⁻].
Neither contains OH⁻ ions, as both are acidic.
It is 100 times smaller in P than in Q.

questions.explanation: [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺]: P 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹, Q 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³. P has 100 times the [H⁺], so 1/100 of the [OH⁻].

questions.stem: Vinegar (ethanoic acid, a weak acid) is in the conical flask. Sodium hydroxide is added from the burette. Which indicator should be used, and what is the colour change at the end point?

options.text: Methyl orange, from red to yellow
Either indicator, because the acid and alkali react in a 1 : 1 ratio
Phenolphthalein, from colourless to pink
Phenolphthalein, from pink to colourless

questions.explanation: Weak acid + strong base: phenolphthalein. It is colourless in the acid and turns pink when a slight excess of alkali is present.

questions.stem: A student mixes two solutions in a polystyrene cup to find an enthalpy change. The thermometer has an uncertainty of ±0.5 °C per reading, and the temperature rises by only about 4 °C. Which change would most reduce the percentage uncertainty in the temperature change, ΔT? -

options.text: Use larger volumes of the same two solutions.
Use more concentrated solutions, keeping the same volumes.
Start with both solutions at a higher temperature.
Record each temperature to two decimal places.

questions.explanation: More reacts in the same volume, so ΔT is larger (e.g. about 20 °C). The ±1.0 °C uncertainty in ΔT is then about 5% instead of 25%.

questions.stem: A student needs the pH of a solution. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Universal indicator gives the pH to two decimal places if the colour is matched carefully.
A pH meter calibrated with buffers of known pH gives a reading to about 0.01 unit.
A pH meter needs no calibration, as its reading is electronic.
Universal indicator is a single indicator that changes colour only at pH 7.

questions.explanation: Calibrated against buffers, a pH meter gives a precise numerical reading, usually to 0.01. Universal indicator only estimates pH.

questions.stem: A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of a weak acid, HA, with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. The student then titrates an identical 25.0 cm³ sample of HA to which 50.0 cm³ of distilled water has been added. How does the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point compare with the first titration, and why?

options.text: It increases, because the flask now holds a larger volume of solution
It is unchanged, because the moles of HA in the flask are unchanged
It decreases, because the HA in the flask is now more dilute
It is unchanged, because adding water does not alter the pH

questions.explanation: Water changes the volume and concentration in the flask, not the moles of HA. The same moles of NaOH, so the same volume, are needed.

questions.stem: A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. A student's titre is 12.50 cm³, found from two readings. What is the percentage uncertainty in the titre?
Two samples of rain are tested with a pH meter. Sample A has pH 4.2; sample B has pH 5.7. How does [H⁺] in sample A compare with [H⁺] in sample B?

options.text: It is 1.5 times greater, as the pH values differ by 1.5.
It is about 15 times greater: 10 times for each pH unit.
It is about 32 times greater.
It is about 32 times smaller, as sample A has the lower pH.

questions.explanation: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, so the ratio is 10⁻⁴·² ÷ 10⁻⁵·⁷ = 10¹·⁵ ≈ 32. Lower pH, more H⁺.

questions.stem: A student records these titres: 24.30 cm³ (rough), 23.85 cm³, 23.40 cm³ and 23.50 cm³. Which mean titre should be used in the calculation?
questions.explanation: Only 23.40 and 23.50 cm³ are concordant (within 0.10 cm³). Their mean is 23.45 cm³.
